references.text: Esau sold his birthright to Jacob, showing that the birthright held great value and significance in patriarchal times.
Esau complains that Jacob has taken both his birthright and his blessing, highlighting the double inheritance portion associated with the birthright.
Jacob gives Joseph an extra share over his brothers, reflecting the principle of a double inheritance for the firstborn.
Jacob describes Reuben as his firstborn, his strength and the first fruit of his vigor, corresponding to the expression 'the beginning of his strength' in Deuteronomy 21:17.
Although Reuben was the firstborn, his birthright was given to Joseph's sons because of his sin, yet the genealogy still follows the order of the firstborn.
Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, alluding to the double inheritance share of the firstborn son.
Esau is described as one who sold his birthright for a single meal, warning against despising God's blessings that the birthright represented.
